Aluminum conducts heat better than cast iron, so heat moves through it faster. That is why a thin aluminum pan heats quickly and responds fast when you raise or lower the burner. In cooking, though, the issue is often not just how fast heat moves, but how much the pan’s temperature drops when cold food hits it.

Cast iron is usually much thicker and heavier than a thin aluminum pan. That extra mass gives it more thermal mass: it stores more heat energy once it has been preheated. When you add cold food, there is more stored heat available at the cooking surface, so the pan resists cooling down as quickly. A thin aluminum pan may transfer heat efficiently, but it has less stored heat to give up.

For example, if you put a cold steak in a well-preheated cast-iron skillet, it often keeps sizzling after the meat hits the surface. In a thin aluminum pan, the surface may lose temperature quickly, and the steak can steam or turn gray before it browns well.

One limitation is that this is not only about the metal. A thick aluminum pan with a heavy base can hold heat much better than a very thin one, and burner power, preheating, and construction all matter.

Think of heat conductivity like a highway. Aluminum is a superhighway—heat zooms through it fast. Cast iron is more like a winding country road. But here’s the kicker: we aren’t talking about speed; we’re talking about storage. 

Cast iron is dense, heavy, and thick. It’s a massive energy sponge. Once you get it hot, it holds onto that thermal energy like a dog with a bone. Aluminum, being lightweight and thin, just doesn't have the physical mass to store much heat, so it cools down the second the flame dies.

Imagine searing a thick ribeye steak. Drop that cold meat into a thin aluminum pan, and the pan’s temperature immediately plummets. You end up graying and steaming the meat instead of getting that gorgeous, crusty sear. In a heavy cast-iron skillet? The pan barely registers the cold steak and just keeps pumping out high heat. (Though, a quick aside: good luck lifting that beast with one hand when it’s full of gravy.)

Of course, this comparison isn't perfect. We’re comparing heavy-duty cast iron to thin, cheap aluminum. A super-thick, professional-grade aluminum pan would hold heat much better, though it still wouldn’t match the sheer heat-retaining muscle of iron.

Look, it’s totally counterintuitive, right? We’re taught that aluminum is the speed demon of the kitchen, whisking heat away from the burner faster than you can say "sauté." And it is. But there’s a massive difference between moving heat quickly and actually holding onto it. Think of it like this: aluminum is a sprinter, while cast iron is a marathon runner with a heavy backpack.

The secret sauce here is thermal mass. Cast iron is dense and thick. It takes a long time to heat up because it needs to soak up a ton of energy, but once it’s hot, it’s got a serious reservoir of thermal energy stored up. Aluminum pans are usually thin and light; they heat up instantly but lose that energy just as fast when you drop in a cold steak.

Picture searing a ribeye. If you use a flimsy aluminum pan, the temperature plummets the second the meat hits the surface, leading to steaming instead of searing. The cast iron? It barely blinks. It dumps its stored heat into the steak, giving you that perfect, crusty exterior.

However, don’t get it twisted. This comparison has a limit: we’re mostly talking about standard, thin-gauge aluminum cookware. If you were using a thick, high-end aluminum core pan, the gap narrows significantly because that extra material adds mass. But for your everyday cheap skillet? Iron wins the endurance test every time.

Marguerite found the book where she always did on Thursdays: wedged between the flour bins and the cooling racks, as if it had climbed in through the wall. *A Field Guide to Coastal Birds*, spine cracked, a faded library stamp inside the cover. Due date long past.

Eleven Thursdays now. She'd asked the day staff, checked the locks, even stayed late once with a thermos and a rolling pin. Nothing. The book simply appeared between two and four a.m., and she never caught the moment.

Tonight it was heavier. She opened it and a folded square of receipt paper slid out.

*I keep meaning to bring it back to the library, but I walk past your window on the way and the light is on, and I think: somebody is awake. Then I leave it here instead. Sorry. I'll stop if you ask me to.*

Marguerite read it twice. Behind her the ovens ticked, and the first trays of rye waited under their cloths.

She turned the receipt over, found a pencil stub behind her ear, and wrote on the back: *Don't stop.* Then she tucked it inside the cover, set the book on the sill by the front window, and left the light on.

Conductivity and heat storage are different properties. Conductivity describes how quickly heat moves through a material. Aluminum is good at this, so a thin aluminum pan heats quickly and spreads heat across its surface. How long a pan stays hot depends mostly on how much heat it has stored, and that depends heavily on mass.

A typical 12-inch cast-iron skillet weighs about 2.5 kilograms. A thin aluminum pan of the same size might weigh under 1 kilogram. Gram for gram, aluminum actually stores roughly twice as much heat as iron, but the cast-iron pan's extra weight more than makes up for that difference. It holds a larger reserve of heat.

You can see this when you put a cold steak in a preheated pan. The steak pulls heat out of the metal right away. A heavy cast-iron skillet loses only part of its reserve, so it keeps searing. A thin aluminum pan has less heat to spare, so its temperature drops sharply and the steak may steam and turn gray. Aluminum also recovers faster once the burner adds heat back.

The comparison has a limit. It holds for heavy cast iron against thin aluminum. A thick aluminum pan of equal weight would store more heat than the iron one.

Think of heat like money. Aluminum is a fast spender: it takes heat from the burner and passes it along quickly to the food. Cast iron is more like a thick savings account. Cast iron takes longer to preheat, but its sheer weight allows it to hold a massive reserve of thermal energy. 

Consider searing a cold steak. Dropping wet meat into thin aluminum instantly saps the pan's heat, causing the steak to stew in its own pooling juices. In contrast, heavy cast iron shrugs off the steak's cold surface, maintaining the high temperature required to instantly brown and crust the meat.

A limitation of this comparison is that it isolates the material while ignoring thickness. A professional-grade, heavy-gauge aluminum pan will retain heat far better than a flimsy sheet of aluminum, narrowing the performance gap. However, pound for pound, typical retail cast iron still wins on pure mass alone.

It might seem counterintuitive that a cast-iron skillet retains heat longer than a thin aluminum pan, given that aluminum is actually a superior thermal conductor. The key difference lies in thermal mass and specific heat capacity, not just conductivity. Cast iron is significantly denser and heavier than thin aluminum. This means it can store a much larger amount of thermal energy for any given temperature. When you place a cold steak into the pan, the cast iron has a vast reservoir of stored heat to draw from, preventing the surface temperature from dropping drastically. In contrast, a thin aluminum pan has very little mass. While it heats up quickly due to high conductivity, it also loses its stored energy rapidly when faced with a cold ingredient, leading to uneven cooking or steaming rather than searing.

Consider searing a thick ribeye steak. A preheated cast-iron skillet will maintain a consistent, high surface temperature throughout the process, creating a perfect, crispy crust. A thin aluminum pan would likely cool down too much upon contact, resulting in a gray, boiled exterior instead of a desirable Maillard reaction. However, this comparison has a limitation: it assumes the aluminum pan is thin. If you were to compare cast iron to a thick, heavy-bottomed aluminum roasting pan, the aluminum might actually retain heat quite well due to its increased mass, narrowing the performance gap significantly. Therefore, thickness and total mass are just as critical as the material itself when evaluating heat retention capabilities in your kitchen tools.

Here's the thing people mix up: conducting heat and *holding* heat aren't the same job. Conductivity is about how fast heat moves through metal. Staying hot is about how much heat the pan has stored up, and that depends mostly on mass.

A thin aluminum skillet might weigh a pound. A 12-inch cast-iron pan? Closer to eight. Even though iron stores less heat per ounce than aluminum (about half, honestly), all that extra metal adds up to a much bigger reservoir of energy. Aluminum's great conductivity just means it spreads heat quickly, and it gives it away quickly too.

You've probably felt this. Drop two cold steaks into a ripping-hot thin pan and the sizzle collapses into a sad hiss; the meat drains the heat faster than the burner can replace it, so you get gray, steamed edges. Do the same in preheated cast iron and the sizzle barely flinches. There's enough stored heat to keep searing while the burner catches up. (This is also why cast iron takes forever to preheat, so it's the same trait working against you.)

The limitation: this compares a heavy pan to a light one, not iron to aluminum. A thick, heavy aluminum pan would hold heat just fine, and pound for pound it'd actually win.

Aluminum conducts heat better than cast iron, so heat moves through an aluminum pan more quickly. That helps the pan respond fast when you turn the burner up or down. But staying hot is not just about how fast heat moves. It also depends on how much heat the pan can store.

A typical cast-iron skillet is much thicker and heavier than a thin aluminum pan. That extra mass acts like a heat reservoir. Once it is fully preheated, it contains more stored heat, so its temperature drops more slowly when you add cold food.

For example, put a room-temperature steak in a hot cast-iron skillet and in a thin aluminum pan. The steak pulls heat out of both pans. The thin aluminum pan may transfer heat into the steak quickly at first, but it has less stored heat, so its surface temperature can fall fast. The cast iron may conduct heat less efficiently, but because it is heavy, it can keep feeding heat into the steak and maintain a stronger sear.

One limitation: this comparison depends on the actual pans. A thick aluminum griddle can store plenty of heat, and a small, thin cast-iron pan may not. Burner size and preheating time also matter.

Even though aluminum conducts heat quickly—meaning it warms up and cools down almost instantly—it lacks the physical mass to store that energy. Cast iron is incredibly dense and heavy. It takes longer to heat up, but once it does, it holds onto that thermal energy like a giant battery.

For a concrete kitchen example, imagine searing a cold, thick ribeye steak. When you drop that cold meat into a thin aluminum pan, the pan’s temperature plummets instantly, causing the steak to steam in its own juices rather than sear. If you drop that same steak into a hot cast-iron skillet, the heavy pan barely registers the cold meat; it retains its intense heat, instantly creating a beautifully caramelized, deep-brown crust.

One limitation of this comparison is that it ignores pan thickness. A incredibly thick, heavy-gauge aluminum pan (like professional cookware) will hold heat much better than a cheap, paper-thin one, though heavy cast iron will still reign supreme in heat retention due to its sheer density.

You could get a whole novel for sixpence. That was the trick Allen Lane pulled off in 1935 when he set up Penguin Books. The price was the same as a packet of cigarettes, and the books looked like it, with colored bands on the spine to sort out the genres. You got the same sort of thing you'd find in a more expensive shop. Some of it was popular fiction, some of it was pretty serious work. You'd already seen the shape of the thing in the pamphlets and chapbooks of the past, and in the yellowbacks of the nineteenth century. But the modern version needed the whole package of mass printing, better paper, and a lot more people who could read. It got into the hands of people on the train, in the classroom, and just out for a walk.

The habit caught on fast, first in Britain and then in the United States and other places. That was mostly during and after the Second World War. The printers cranked out the novels, the biographies, the mysteries and romances, and the school books. A soldier, a student, or a working person could put together a library that way. Nobody else could have afforded the same collection. By the middle of the last century that had become the main way people got hold of books. You've still got it to hand now.
